title: Jim James Tries to Get Found on New Solo Song ‘Lost Child’
summary: Track will appear on upcoming album, Wowed Out, due Friday
whatHappening: Jim James, the primary songwriter and vocalist of My Morning Jacket, has released a new solo song titled 'Lost Child.' The track will appear on his upcoming album, Wowed Out, arriving this Friday.
whoInvolved: Jim James (James Edward Olliges Jr.) is an American vocalist, guitarist, and producer best known as the primary songwriter of the rock band My Morning Jacket, formed in Louisville, Kentucky in 1998. My Morning Jacket is an experimental, psychedelic rock band that built a significant following beginning in the 2000s, partly through their acclaimed live performances.
whyMatters: The release signals continued solo activity from James alongside his work with My Morning Jacket, demonstrating his ongoing creative output across multiple projects. The album drop this Friday marks a notable moment for fans of both his solo work and the broader My Morning Jacket universe.
articleBody:
Jim James is stepping into the spotlight with a new solo single as his upcoming album approaches release. 'Lost Child,' according to Rolling Stone, will be featured on Wowed Out, an album set to arrive this Friday. The track represents James's latest foray into solo material, continuing a pattern of artistic expansion beyond his primary role in My Morning Jacket.

James, professionally known as Jim James or Yim Yames, has established himself as a multifaceted musician throughout his career. As the vocalist, guitarist, and primary songwriter of My Morning Jacket—the Louisville-based rock band he has anchored since its formation in 1998—James has helped shape the group's distinctive sound, which blends rock and country influences with experimental and psychedelic elements. The band, rounded out by bassist Tom Blankenship, drummer Patrick Hallahan, guitarist Carl Broemel, and keyboardist Bo Koster, built a devoted following beginning in the 2000s in part due to their reputation for dynamic live performances.

Beyond My Morning Jacket, James has also pursued a parallel solo career, releasing several albums that allow him to explore different creative directions. This solo work has given him space to develop his production skills and songwriting voice independently, complementing rather than competing with his responsibilities in the band. The forthcoming album Wowed Out appears to continue this tradition of independent artistic expression.

The release of 'Lost Child' comes as James prepares to share the full scope of Wowed Out with listeners this week. With the album's imminent arrival, the single serves as a preview of what fans can expect from his latest body of solo work. The track's title suggests themes of searching and displacement, potentially offering insight into the album's broader thematic concerns.

title: Johnny Marr Finds Defiance in Idealism on New Single ‘It’s Time’
summary: The Smiths guitarist will release his fifth solo album, The Age of Everything, in October
whatHappening: Johnny Marr, legendary guitarist of The Smiths, has released a new single titled 'It's Time' that showcases idealistic themes. The track arrives ahead of his fifth solo album, The Age of Everything, set for October release.
whoInvolved: Johnny Marr is an English-born Irish musician best known as guitarist and co-songwriter of The Smiths, the influential Manchester rock band active from 1982 to 1987. He has maintained a prolific solo career alongside work with numerous other bands since the group's split.
whyMatters: The release marks another significant milestone in Marr's solo trajectory and signals continued artistic evolution nearly four decades after The Smiths' original run. For fans of one of British rock's most important bands, new solo material demonstrates that Marr remains creatively engaged and willing to explore contemporary themes through his distinctive guitar work.
articleBody:
Johnny Marr continues to cement his solo legacy with the release of 'It's Time,' a new single that finds the storied guitarist channeling defiance through idealistic messaging. According to Rolling Stone, the track precedes Marr's fifth solo album, The Age of Everything, which is scheduled for October release.

Marr first rose to prominence as the guitarist and co-songwriter of The Smiths, the Manchester-formed rock band that operated from 1982 to 1987. Alongside vocalist Morrissey, Marr crafted the songwriting partnership that would define the band's sound and help establish The Smiths as one of the most important British acts of their era and pioneers of 1980s independent music. The group's original lineup also included bassist Andy Rourke and drummer Mike Joyce.

Since The Smiths' dissolution, Marr has maintained an active presence in music, performing with numerous bands and building an extensive solo career across multiple decades. The forthcoming album represents his fifth solo venture, underscoring his consistent output and refusal to rest on the band's considerable legacy.

'It's Time' appears positioned as a statement piece for the new record, with its thematic focus on idealism suggesting Marr remains engaged with substantive lyrical content. The single's title and thematic direction hint at both introspection and conviction, qualities that have characterized much of his post-Smiths work.

The Age of Everything marks another chapter in what has become a remarkably durable solo career. For listeners who followed The Smiths' influential run through the 1980s independent music landscape, Marr's continued creative output demonstrates a willingness to evolve while maintaining the artistic standards that defined his earlier work.

articleBody:

According to Rolling Stone, the artist made direct remarks to Donald Trump about losing weight, framing the suggestion in personal terms and emphasizing potential physical benefits.

Jelly Roll's remarks exemplify a broader pattern of celebrities using late-night television to engage directly with political figures on matters of public interest. The comment arrives amid ongoing public scrutiny of political figures' health and fitness levels, a recurring element of modern political discourse. title: Watch Van Halen’s Michael Anthony Play ‘Runnin’ With The Devil’ With Jason Bonham
summary: It was the first time in the 16-year history of Jason Bonham's Led Zeppelin Evening that a song not found in the Zeppelin catalog was performed at one of their shows
whatHappening: Michael Anthony, bassist for Van Halen, performed 'Runnin' With The Devil'—a Van Halen classic—alongside Jason Bonham at one of Bonham's Led Zeppelin tribute shows. It marked a historic first: the 16-year-old Led Zeppelin Evening had never featured a song outside the Zeppelin catalog until this performance.
whoInvolved: Michael Anthony is the bassist for Van Halen, the legendary American rock band formed in Pasadena in 1972 and credited with restoring hard rock to mainstream prominence. Jason Bonham is the son of John Bonham, Led Zeppelin's original drummer, and has spent 16 years headlining the Led Zeppelin Evening, a tribute show celebrating his father's legendary band.
whyMatters: The performance represents a rare departure from the strict setlist boundaries that have defined Jason Bonham's Led Zeppelin Evening for nearly two decades, signaling a willingness to expand the show's scope. It also underscores the shared musical DNA between Van Halen and Led Zeppelin, two foundational acts in rock history whose combined influence shaped generations of musicians.
articleBody:
Michael Anthony brought a piece of Van Halen's catalog to Jason Bonham's Led Zeppelin Evening when he joined the tribute show to perform 'Runnin' With The Devil,' marking a watershed moment in the 16-year history of Bonham's traveling exhibition of his father's legendary material. According to Rolling Stone, the performance was the first time a song outside the Led Zeppelin catalog had been featured at one of these events.

Jason Bonham has spent the better part of two decades curating these shows as a celebration of his father, John Bonham, who was the drummer for Led Zeppelin from the band's 1968 formation in London through their 1980 dissolution. Led Zeppelin, comprising vocalist Robert Plant, guitarist Jimmy Page, bassist and keyboardist John Paul Jones, and John Bonham on drums, pioneered the synthesis of heavy electric rock with blues and folk influences that became the template for hard rock and heavy metal itself. Their cultural footprint remains immense—they are among the best-selling music artists of all time.

Van Halen, formed in Pasadena, California in 1972, carved out their own towering legacy by restoring hard rock to the forefront of the music scene during an era when the genre needed reinvention. The band became known for electrifying live performances and the virtuosic guitar work of Eddie Van Halen, whose technical innovations influenced countless players. 'Runnin' With The Devil,' one of Van Halen's signature tracks, represents the hard-hitting energy and musicianship that defined their career.

Michael Anthony's appearance at the Led Zeppelin Evening underscores an implicit kinship between the two bands. Both Van Halen and Led Zeppelin occupied the upper echelon of rock's power hierarchy, commanding massive audiences and shaping the sound of their respective eras. By stepping onto the stage to perform Van Halen material within the framework of Bonham's tribute, Anthony created a symbolic convergence of two lineages that, while distinct in style, share common roots in blues-inflected hard rock and virtuoso musicianship.

The decision to break the Led Zeppelin-only tradition suggests that Jason Bonham may be open to occasional guest appearances and musical detours that honor the broader rock pantheon while maintaining the show's primary focus. Such moments are rare enough in a long-running tribute series that they become memorable for fans and musicians alike, creating unexpected connections between artists and eras that shaped rock history.

title: Television’s Richard Lloyd Diagnosed With Cancer
summary: “I am taking this in stride, but it has become very difficult on our own and financially we are strapped,” says the guitarist
whatHappening: Richard Lloyd, guitarist for the influential 1970s rock band Television, has been diagnosed with cancer. He is facing both health challenges and financial strain as he navigates treatment.
whoInvolved: Richard Lloyd is the guitarist for Television, an American rock band formed in New York City in 1973 that became a foundational influence on punk and alternative rock. The band's classic lineup included Tom Verlaine, Lloyd, drummer Billy Ficca, and bassist Fred Smith, and they were early fixtures of the legendary CBGB club.
whyMatters: Lloyd's diagnosis highlights the vulnerability of aging musicians from influential eras who may lack robust financial safety nets. The situation underscores how health crises can compound existing financial pressures for artists, particularly those from earlier decades before modern touring economics and streaming revenue.
articleBody:
Richard Lloyd, the guitarist for Television, has been diagnosed with cancer, according to Pitchfork. In discussing his condition, Lloyd acknowledged the difficulty of managing both his health and his household finances. "I am taking this in stride, but it has become very difficult on our own and financially we are strapped," he said.

Lloyd rose to prominence as a member of Television, the pioneering rock band formed in New York City in 1973. Alongside vocalist and guitarist Tom Verlaine, drummer Billy Ficca, and bassist Fred Smith, Lloyd helped shape the sound of punk and alternative rock during the band's early years as fixtures of the CBGB scene in the mid-1970s. The group is widely recognized as influential in the development of both genres, with their innovative guitar work and art-rock sensibilities marking a departure from the three-chord simplicity often associated with early punk.

The diagnosis comes at a time when Lloyd faces financial constraints related to his treatment and care. His candid remarks about the strain suggest that managing a serious illness without adequate resources has become an immediate concern for him and his family. Many musicians from Television's era have faced financial challenges in later life, particularly those who did not achieve sustained commercial success over the course of their careers.

Television's legacy has endured through decades of influence on subsequent generations of musicians, though the band's direct commercial success was more modest than some of their contemporaries. Lloyd's struggle highlights the broader reality that even influential artists from seminal bands may not have secured the financial stability needed to weather major health crises without difficulty.

title: Bret Michaels Cancels All 2026 Tour Dates for ‘Rest and Recovery’ After Recent Surgeries
summary: "I may have just chosen to go sooner than I should have," singer writes after comeback show following kidney stone removal. "We will come back better than ever"
whatHappening: Bret Michaels is canceling all 2026 tour dates to prioritize rest and recovery following recent surgeries, including kidney stone removal. The decision comes after the Poison frontman performed a comeback show, which he now acknowledges may have been premature.
whoInvolved: Bret Michaels is the frontman of Poison, the rock band that has sold over 65 million albums worldwide and charted 10 singles to the Billboard Hot 100, including the number-one hit "Every Rose Has Its Thorn." He is managing his health following surgical procedures.
whyMatters: The cancellation signals potential ongoing health challenges for a major touring artist in his sixties and may disappoint fans expecting shows next year. It underscores the physical toll of intensive touring and recovery from serious medical procedures, particularly for established acts balancing legacy commitments with health needs.
articleBody:
Bret Michaels, the frontman of legendary rock band Poison, has announced the cancellation of all tour dates scheduled for 2026, citing the need for continued rest and recovery following recent surgeries. The decision comes on the heels of a comeback performance that Michaels now feels may have been rushed, prompting him to take a more measured approach to his touring schedule.

Michaels, who leads Poison—a band that has sold over 65 million albums worldwide and achieved major chart success with hits including the number-one single "Every Rose Has Its Thorn"—underwent kidney stone removal prior to his recent comeback show. According to Rolling Stone, the singer acknowledged in a statement that he "may have just chosen to go sooner than I should have," suggesting that returning to the stage so quickly after surgery took a greater toll than anticipated.

The 2026 cancellation represents a significant step back for touring plans that had presumably been in development. Rather than risk further complications, Michaels is prioritizing his physical well-being and committing to a longer recovery timeline. In his statement, he assured fans that "we will come back better than ever," signaling optimism about eventual future performances once his health is fully restored.

For a touring musician of Michaels' stature and history, the decision to cancel an entire year of dates is substantial. Poison has built its legacy on live performances and has charted 10 singles to the Billboard Hot 100, including six Top 10 hits, making touring a core part of the band's identity and revenue. The cancellation reflects the physical demands that intensive touring places on performers, particularly as they age.

Michaels' transparent communication about his decision—acknowledging that he pushed too hard too soon—provides insight into the complex calculus performers face when balancing health concerns against career momentum and fan expectations. By committing to extended recovery rather than attempting a reduced 2026 schedule, he is prioritizing long-term health sustainability over short-term performance commitments.

title: ZZ Top Play First Show Since Death of ‘Dear Drummer’ Frank Beard
summary: "We’re all here for a celebration, you know what's going on. So we're gonna have a good time," Billy Gibbons told Austin crowd as band returned to stage following Beard's death earlier this week
whatHappening: ZZ Top returned to the stage in Austin for their first performance since the death of drummer Frank Beard earlier this week. Billy Gibbons told the crowd they were gathered for a celebration, signaling the band's determination to honor their late bandmate by continuing to perform.
whoInvolved: ZZ Top is an iconic American rock band formed in Houston in 1969, consisting of vocalist-guitarist Billy Gibbons, drummer Frank Beard, and bassist-vocalist Dusty Hill until Hill's death in 2021. Beard, who passed away in 2026 after five decades with the band, was a cornerstone of their signature blues-based sound.
whyMatters: Beard's death marks a watershed moment for one of rock's most enduring acts, bringing an end to an era of nearly uninterrupted lineup stability spanning five decades. The band's immediate return to performing signals their commitment to their legacy and fanbase, even as they face the challenge of continuing without a founding member.
articleBody:
ZZ Top played their first show since the death of drummer Frank Beard, taking the stage in Austin as Billy Gibbons addressed the crowd with a message of unity and remembrance. "We're all here for a celebration, you know what's going on. So we're gonna have a good time," Gibbons told the audience, according to Rolling Stone, setting the tone for a performance dedicated to honoring their late bandmate.

Beard's passing this week marked the end of an extraordinary chapter in rock history. The drummer had been with ZZ Top since the band's formation in Houston, Texas, in 1969, making him a foundational element of their sound for nearly five decades. Along with bassist-vocalist Dusty Hill, Beard formed the rhythm section that anchored Billy Gibbons' distinctive blues-influenced guitar work, helping ZZ Top develop the signature sound that made them one of rock's most recognizable acts.

The band's lineup had remained remarkably stable throughout their career until recent years. Dusty Hill's death in 2021 was the first significant change to the trio's composition, and Beard's death in 2026 represents the loss of the final surviving founding member alongside Gibbons. The drummer was known not only for his technical contributions but also for being an integral part of the band's visual identity and stage presence.

ZZ Top built their reputation over decades on a foundation of live performances, sly and humorous lyrics, and a carefully cultivated image that became iconic in rock culture. Beard's role as the "dear drummer," as he was affectionately referred to, was essential to the chemistry that made their concerts legendary. His passing leaves Gibbons navigating the future of the band at a pivotal moment.

By returning to Austin so quickly after Beard's death, ZZ Top demonstrated their commitment to their fans and their legacy. The choice to frame the performance as a celebration rather than a somber farewell reflects the band's approach to honoring their late drummer while maintaining the spirit of live rock and roll that has defined their career. For longtime fans and the Austin community where the band originated, this performance represented both a time of grief and a reaffirmation of the enduring impact of ZZ Top's music.

title: Deep Cuts, Hits, and a Choir: Foo Fighters’ Hollywood Bowl Debut Sends Off Gustavo Dudamel With a Bang
summary: The band also paid tribute to late drummer Taylor Hawkins in a short, effective set
whatHappening: Foo Fighters performed at the Hollywood Bowl, blending deep cuts with hits and featuring a choir to honor departing conductor Gustavo Dudamel. The band also paid tribute to late drummer Taylor Hawkins during the concert.
whoInvolved: Foo Fighters is an American rock band formed in Seattle in 1994 by former Nirvana drummer Dave Grohl, who remains the vocalist and guitarist alongside bassist Nate Mendel, guitarists Pat Smear and Chris Shiflett, keyboardist Rami Jaffee, and drummer Ilan Rubin. The concert honored Taylor Hawkins, the band's longtime drummer who joined in 1997 and died in March 2022 after recording eight studio albums with the group.
whyMatters: The performance marks a significant moment for both the band and the Los Angeles cultural institution, serving as a farewell celebration for Dudamel's tenure while allowing Foo Fighters to publicly memorialize a key member of their lineup. Such high-profile tributes help keep Hawkins' legacy alive within the rock community and demonstrate how major artists continue to process grief through their craft.
articleBody:
Foo Fighters took the stage at the Hollywood Bowl to deliver a concert that balanced the band's extensive catalog with ceremonial significance, marking a special farewell for conductor Gustavo Dudamel. The setlist drew from across the band's discography, mixing fan favorites with deeper cuts, while a choir added orchestral texture to the performance. According to Rolling Stone, the band also incorporated a short but effective tribute to Taylor Hawkins, their drummer who passed away in March 2022.

Hawkins had been central to Foo Fighters' sound for over two decades. He joined the Seattle rock band in 1997, just three years after Dave Grohl founded it as a solo project following his departure from Nirvana. During his tenure, Hawkins not only played drums but also shared vocal duties with Grohl, contributing to eight studio albums recorded between 1999 and 2021. His sudden death left a significant void in the band's lineup and in the broader rock music community.

The Hollywood Bowl show represented more than a standard concert performance. By pairing the musical event with a tribute to Hawkins and a ceremonial send-off for Dudamel, the evening took on added weight as a moment of collective remembrance. The inclusion of a choir elevated the production beyond the band's typical live format, transforming the bowl into a venue for both rock performance and formal tribute.

Foo Fighters have continued performing and recording since Hawkins' death, adapting their live setup with new drummer Ilan Rubin. The band's willingness to honor Hawkins at major performances like the Hollywood Bowl shows underscores his lasting impact on their identity and legacy. Each tribute keeps his memory present for longtime fans while introducing newer listeners to the depth of his contributions.

The concert also marked a cultural milestone for the Hollywood Bowl itself, which serves as one of the nation's premier outdoor performance venues. Dudamel's departure represents a significant transition for the institution, and Foo Fighters' high-profile tribute concert provided a noteworthy moment during that period of change. Such collaborations between rock bands and classical institutions highlight the increasingly fluid boundaries between different musical worlds in contemporary performance.

articleBody:

Don Toliver has emerged as a rising force in hip-hop following his 2018 debut mixtape Donny Womack and subsequent collaborations with major artists. The Miami performance itself represents a notable moment for concert culture, where surprise guest appearances continue to generate significant fan engagement and social media buzz. Fans and industry observers will likely watch for further announcements about Timberlake's touring plans, given the significance of this return to the stage. The collaboration also underscores the contemporary music landscape, where pop and hip-hop artists frequently share stages and audiences.

title: See King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard Bring Out Max Weinberg at Queens Show

whatHappening: Max Weinberg, the legendary E Street Band drummer, took the stage at King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard's Forest Hills Stadium concert in Queens, stepping in as a special guest. The iconic drummer filled in for Jay Weinberg, his son and a friend of the Australian psych-rock band.

King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard is an Australian rock band formed in Melbourne in 2010, known for their energetic live performances and prolific output across multiple genres.
whyMatters: The appearance represents a rare cross-generational and cross-genre collaboration, bringing together a classic rock legend with a contemporary psych-rock act. articleBody:

According to Rolling Stone, Weinberg filled in for Jay Weinberg, his son and a friend of the band, in a moment that bridged classic and contemporary rock worlds.

The band's current lineup includes Stu Mackenzie, Ambrose Kenny-Smith, Cook Craig, Joey Walker, Lucas Harwood, and Michael Cavanagh. Their willingness to invite special guests to their performances reflects the collaborative ethos that has defined their approach to live music.

Max Weinberg's appearance carried particular significance given his decades-long tenure as the heartbeat of the E Street Band. Beyond his work with Springsteen, Weinberg has maintained a high profile as a television personality, serving as bandleader for Conan O'Brien on both Late Night and The Tonight Show. His participation in the Forest Hills show demonstrated the kind of spontaneous collaboration that energizes live rock performances and creates memorable moments for audiences.

Jay Weinberg, Max's son, has established his own drumming credentials, having worked with both Slipknot and Suicidal Tendencies. His friendship with King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard, strong enough to make him a regular part of their live performances, created the circumstances for Max's guest appearance. The intergenerational dynamic—with the elder Weinberg stepping in for his son—added an extra layer of meaning to an already notable moment.

The Queens concert showcased the kind of cross-genre pollination that continues to define rock music in the contemporary landscape, where established legends and emerging acts frequently find common ground on stage. For audiences at Forest Hills Stadium, the evening provided an unexpected encounter with one of rock's most accomplished and enduring drummers.

articleBody:

Artists facing criminal charges often confront additional complications beyond immediate legal consequences, including potential travel restrictions, bail conditions, or court appearances that can interfere with tour commitments. title: Janie Bradford, Motown Songwriter Who Co-Wrote ‘Money (That’s What I Want’), Dead at 87
summary: "Janie was there with me from the very beginning, before there was even a Motown," Berry Gordy writes in tribute to label's receptionist-turned-hit songwriter
whatHappening: Janie Bradford, the pioneering Motown songwriter and receptionist who co-wrote the enduring hit 'Money (That's What I Want)', has died at 87. Berry Gordy, Motown's founder, paid tribute to her as a foundational figure in the label's early history.
whoInvolved: Janie Bradford was an American songwriter who rose from receptionist to hit-maker at Motown Records, the Detroit-based label founded by Berry Gordy Jr. in 1959. Bradford's most famous collaboration with Gordy, 'Money', became a standard recorded by artists including Barrett Strong, The Beatles, and The Rolling Stones.
whyMatters: Bradford's death marks the passing of a key architect of Motown's sound during its formative years, when the label was establishing itself as a powerhouse of American popular music. Her songwriting legacy, particularly 'Money', has endured across generations and genres, influencing rock, pop, and soul music for over six decades.
articleBody:
Janie Bradford, a songwriter who helped shape Motown Records' golden era and co-wrote one of popular music's most recorded songs, has died at 87. Berry Gordy, the legendary founder of Motown, paid homage to Bradford's irreplaceable role in the label's creation, writing that "Janie was there with me from the very beginning, before there was even a Motown."

Bradford began her career at Motown as a receptionist, a position that placed her at the heart of the nascent label during its earliest days. Founded by Gordy as Tamla Records on January 12, 1959, and incorporated as Motown Record Corporation on April 14, 1960, the Detroit-based operation was still finding its footing when Bradford joined. Her ascent from front-desk duties to songwriter reflects both her talent and the fluid, entrepreneurial environment Gordy cultivated at the label whose name became synonymous with Detroit itself.

Bradford's most enduring contribution to music came through her collaboration with Gordy on "Money (That's What I Want)." Originally recorded by Barrett Strong, the song became a template for what Motown would become: a bridge between rhythm and blues and mainstream pop. According to Rolling Stone, the track's infectious groove and straightforward lyrical hook made it irresistible to artists across genres. The song entered the rock canon when The Beatles recorded it for their second album, "With The Beatles," and it also appeared on The Rolling Stones' first UK EP, cementing its status as a standard.

What made "Money" remarkable was its staying power. Decades after its initial release, the song continued to be recorded and reimagined by successive generations of musicians, a testament to both Bradford and Gordy's songwriting acumen. The track transcended the soul and R&B markets where it originated, becoming a touchstone in rock and pop music—a rare achievement that underscored Bradford's gift for crafting hooks and narratives that resonated across audiences.

Bradford's career at Motown reflected a broader pattern within the label: talented individuals found opportunities to grow and contribute across multiple roles. While she may not have achieved the household-name status of some Motown artists, her influence rippled through the label's output and, by extension, through popular music itself. Her presence during Motown's formative period made her a custodian of the label's creative spirit during the years when it was establishing the sound that would define a generation.

whyMatters: The exclusive physical release strategy highlights how artists are leveraging independent record retailers to build buzz and create scarcity around new music. articleBody:

Anolog Music Shop's selection as the exclusive first retail outlet is particularly notable given its proximity to Rodrigo's Daisy Chain Fields. articleBody:

title: Tupac Jurors See Keffe D’s First Public Interview About Killing: ‘I Got Cancer…Nothing Else to Lose’
summary: The jury also heard Keffe claim in a 2009 police interview that alleged gunman Orlando Anderson “peed on his hands” after the shooting to wash away gunpowder
whatHappening: Jurors in the Tupac Shakur murder trial are hearing testimony from Keffe D, a key witness who has now given his first public interview detailing his account of the 1996 killing. In a 2009 police interview played for the court, Keffe D claims that alleged gunman Orlando Anderson used an unusual method to dispose of evidence after the shooting.
whoInvolved: Keffe D is a witness in the case involving the murder of Tupac Shakur, the influential rapper and activist who was shot in a drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, in Las Vegas. Orlando Anderson is identified as the alleged gunman in the case that has remained unsolved for nearly three decades.
whyMatters: This testimony represents a major development in one of hip-hop's most infamous unsolved murders, offering potential breakthrough evidence after 28 years. The trial outcome could finally provide closure to Tupac's family and fans while setting a significant precedent for cold-case prosecution in high-profile crimes.
articleBody:
Jurors in the long-awaited trial over Tupac Shakur's 1996 murder are now seeing evidence from Keffe D, a witness whose testimony may finally shed light on one of the music industry's most enduring mysteries. According to Rolling Stone, the jury heard a 2009 police interview in which Keffe D claims that alleged gunman Orlando Anderson engaged in an unusual attempt to cover his tracks immediately after the shooting—specifically, that Anderson "peed on his hands" to wash away gunpowder residue.

On September 7, 1996, at 11:15 p.m., Tupac Shakur, then 25 years old, was struck by four rounds from a .40-caliber Glock 22 pistol in a drive-by shooting at a Las Vegas intersection. The shots hit Shakur twice in the chest, once in the arm, and once in the thigh. Suge Knight, the driver of Shakur's vehicle, was grazed by a bullet during the attack. Shakur died six days later from his injuries, and the case went cold for nearly three decades.

Keffe D's willingness to testify publicly now appears tied to his health. In the interview, he reportedly stated "I got cancer… nothing else to lose," suggesting that his terminal diagnosis has motivated him to finally speak openly about the circumstances of the shooting. This kind of deathbed confession or late-life testimony has occasionally broken open cold cases where witnesses previously feared retaliation or other consequences.

The specificity of Keffe D's account—including the detail about Anderson's method of attempting to remove gunpowder evidence—provides investigators with forensic and behavioral details that could corroborate or contradict other evidence presented in the trial. Such granular testimony is often crucial in cases where decades have passed and physical evidence may have degraded or been lost.

Tupac Shakur was one of the most influential musical artists of the 20th century, a rapper and actor whose work addressed social injustice and the marginalization of African Americans, though he was also closely associated with gangsta rap. His death at 25 cut short the career of an artist who had already sold millions of records and established himself as both a cultural and political voice. The unsolved nature of his murder has cast a long shadow over hip-hop history, making this trial a potential turning point in a case that has remained open longer than most homicides.

title: Tupac Murder Trial: Jurors Hear ‘Secret’ Police Interview with Keffe D Admitting Role in Shooting
summary: Duane “Keffe D” Davis now says he lied to investigators during the meeting to gain leverage while facing a potential life sentence on drug charges
whatHappening: Jurors in the Tupac Shakur murder trial are hearing testimony from a secret police interview in which Duane "Keffe D" Davis admitted to a role in the 1994 shooting. Davis now claims he lied during that interview to gain leverage while facing potential life imprisonment on drug charges.
whoInvolved: Duane Davis, also known as Keffe D, is a figure connected to the decades-old murder of Tupac Shakur, one of the most influential rappers and cultural activists of the 20th century who sold over 75 million records worldwide. The case involves law enforcement investigators seeking to finally resolve one of hip-hop's most infamous unsolved murders.
whyMatters: The trial represents a rare moment of potential closure in a case that has captivated the public for nearly three decades. The credibility of Davis's statements—whether his admission or his current denial—will be central to whether the murder can finally be prosecuted, making the jury's assessment of his truthfulness potentially decisive in achieving justice for Shakur's death.
articleBody:
Jurors in the murder trial related to Tupac Shakur's death are being presented with a recorded police interview in which Duane "Keffe D" Davis detailed his involvement in the 1994 shooting that killed the legendary rapper. According to Rolling Stone, Davis now claims he intentionally lied to investigators during that encounter, asserting that he provided the false admission to gain leverage in his own legal situation as he faced the prospect of a life sentence on drug charges.

Tupac Amaru Shakur, known by his stage names 2Pac and Makaveli, was an American rapper and actor who became one of the most influential musical artists of the 20th century. His murder on the Las Vegas Strip in September 1994 remained officially unsolved for nearly three decades, making it one of hip-hop's most persistent mysteries. Shakur's body of work addressed social injustice and political issues affecting African Americans, and he sold more than 75 million records worldwide, cementing his status as a cultural icon far beyond music.

The introduction of the secret interview recording into trial proceedings presents a complex evidentiary puzzle for jurors. On one hand, Davis appears on the recording admitting to a role in the shooting—a confession that could be viewed as highly incriminating. On the other hand, his current claim that he fabricated the admission to manipulate investigators creates reasonable doubt about whether any statements he made during that interview can be trusted. This contradiction places the jury in the position of determining not only what happened nearly thirty years ago, but also assessing the credibility and motivation of a key witness whose own account of his actions has fundamentally shifted.

Davis's assertion that he lied to gain leverage reflects a common defense strategy in criminal cases, where defendants or witnesses claim they made false statements under pressure or to achieve some tactical advantage. The drug charges Davis faced at the time of the interview add context to his potential motivation—with his freedom and future at stake, a calculated admission might have seemed a worthwhile trade-off. However, the very fact that he had motive to lie then raises questions about his current testimony and motivations as well.

The trial marks a significant moment in the long-stalled investigation into Shakur's death. For decades, the case languished as a cold file, with no arrests or convictions despite numerous theories and suspects. The decision to finally prosecute, based substantially on Davis's involvement and testimony, suggests that authorities believed they had finally gathered sufficient evidence to move forward. Whether the jury will accept Davis's current version of events or weigh his recorded admission as more credible remains to be seen.

title: Alex Lifeson Quit Weed for Rush’s Tour. These 10 Musicians Gave It Up, Too (Or At Least Tried)

whoInvolved: Alex Lifeson is the guitarist and co-founder of Rush, the legendary Canadian rock band formed in Toronto in 1968. Rush maintained its classic three-member lineup of Lifeson, Geddy Lee, and Neil Peart from 1974 until the band's initial dissolution in 2015, eventually reforming in 2025.

articleBody:
Alex Lifeson has made the decision to quit marijuana as Rush prepares for its upcoming tour, joining a notable group of musicians who have taken similar steps. The guitarist and co-founder of Rush, one of rock's most enduring acts, is prioritizing sobriety ahead of what will be a significant moment for the band that has commanded devoted audiences since its formation in Toronto in 1968.

Lifeson's choice is far from unique in the music world. According to Rolling Stone, a range of high-profile artists have publicly discussed quitting cannabis or attempting to do so, including Miley Cyrus, Willie Nelson, Paul McCartney, and SZA. The magazine compiled a list of ten musicians with similar stories, underscoring that this decision crosses genre lines and career stages.

Rush itself carries particular weight in rock history. The band's classic lineup—Lifeson on guitar alongside Geddy Lee on bass and vocals and Neil Peart on drums—took shape in 1974 and remained unchanged for more than four decades until the band's initial dissolution in 2015. That stability and longevity made Rush a powerhouse in progressive rock, known for technical virtuosity and elaborate compositions that demanded peak cognitive performance from all members.

For touring musicians, the physical and mental demands are substantial. Extended travel, nightly performances, and the need for precision in complex arrangements all benefit from clarity and focus. Lifeson's decision to eliminate cannabis use before hitting the road reflects a practical reassessment of what his body and mind require to deliver the performances that Rush's audience expects.

The willingness of musicians across different genres and generations to discuss their substance use—whether quitting, reducing, or maintaining—marks a shift in how the industry talks about these issues. Where previous decades saw drug use largely treated as part of rock mythology, contemporary artists are more candid about making deliberate health choices. This transparency may encourage fans and younger musicians to examine their own habits without shame.

As Lifeson and Rush prepare for their tour, the guitarist's decision serves as a reminder that even veteran performers continuously reassess their personal practices in service of their craft.

title: Green Day’s Mike Dirnt to Sell One-of-a-Kind Bass Guitars, Clothing, More on Reverb
summary: Collection includes Dookie, Nimrod, and American Idiot-era bass guitars, alongside other gear and clothing spanning musician's career on Reverb
whatHappening: Mike Dirnt, bassist and co-founder of Green Day, is selling a curated collection of his personal bass guitars, gear, and clothing through Reverb, the online marketplace for musical instruments. The collection spans decades of the band's career, including iconic instruments from the Dookie, Nimrod, and American Idiot eras.
whoInvolved: Mike Dirnt is the co-founder, bassist, and backing vocalist of Green Day, the American rock band formed in 1987 in Rodeo, California. Reverb is a major online platform specializing in buying and selling musical instruments and gear.
whyMatters: This sale offers fans and collectors rare access to instruments central to some of punk rock's most defining albums, while also reflecting a growing trend of legacy artists monetizing memorabilia. For Dirnt personally, the sale represents a curated dispersal of career artifacts that might otherwise remain private or undocumented.
articleBody:
Mike Dirnt, the bassist and co-founder of Green Day, is opening up his personal archive to fans and collectors through a special sale on Reverb, the online marketplace for musical instruments and gear. According to Rolling Stone, the collection includes bass guitars from the band's most celebrated album eras—Dookie, Nimrod, and American Idiot—along with additional equipment and clothing that chronicle Dirnt's decades-long career in one of punk rock's most influential bands.

Green Day formed in Rodeo, California, in 1987, with Dirnt and lead singer Billie Joe Armstrong as founding members; drummer Tré Cool joined in 1990. The band achieved massive commercial success with their 1994 major-label debut Dookie, released through Reprise Records, which became a breakout phenomenon and eventually shipped over 20 million copies in the United States alone. That album, along with subsequent releases like Nimrod and the Grammy-winning American Idiot, helped reignite mainstream interest in punk rock and cemented Green Day's place as one of the defining rock bands of their generation.

The bass guitars being offered on Reverb represent tangible connections to those pivotal moments in rock history. Each instrument carries the sonic and visual history of the records and tours that shaped modern punk, making them particularly valuable to dedicated fans and serious collectors. By choosing Reverb as the sales platform, Dirnt is tapping into a community of musicians and enthusiasts who actively buy, sell, and trade professional-grade equipment and rare instruments.

Beyond the guitars, the sale encompasses a broader range of memorabilia reflecting Dirnt's career trajectory. Clothing and other gear spanning his time with Green Day offer fans additional touchpoints to the musician's professional journey. This approach of offering diverse items rather than a single-item auction allows collectors at different levels of investment to potentially acquire something meaningful.

The sale underscores a shift in how legacy musicians approach their personal archives, moving from private storage to public market accessibility. Rather than keeping career artifacts locked away, Dirnt's decision to make them available on a mainstream platform democratizes access to pieces of music history. For those who grew up listening to Dookie or who discovered Green Day through American Idiot, owning an instrument that helped create those soundtracks represents a direct bridge between listener and artist.

title: Suge Knight Gang Associate Dodges Questions at Tupac Trial: ‘Not Gonna Send Him to Prison’
summary: Former gang member James McDonald testified at the trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis
whatHappening: A former gang member testified at the trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis, the man accused of killing Tupac Shakur in 1994, but refused to answer key questions that could implicate him in the crime. The witness, James McDonald, invoked his right against self-incrimination during cross-examination.
whoInvolved: Duane "Keffe D" Davis is on trial for the 1994 murder of Tupac Amaru Shakur, one of the most influential rappers and cultural figures of the 20th century. James McDonald, a former gang associate connected to Suge Knight's circle, was called to testify but resisted providing incriminating details about the shooting.
whyMatters: This testimony marks a critical moment in the decades-long effort to solve Tupac's murder, one of hip-hop's most infamous unsolved cases. The reluctance of witnesses to fully cooperate underscores the lingering code of silence among gang members and the challenges prosecutors face in securing convictions in cases rooted in street violence from three decades ago.
articleBody:
A former gang member took the stand at the trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis on accusations related to the 1994 murder of Tupac Shakur, but repeatedly refused to answer prosecutors' questions, citing his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination. James McDonald's testimony revealed the persistent obstacles courts face when pursuing convictions in decades-old cases involving street violence and gang networks.

Tupac Shakur, known by his stage names 2Pac and Makaveli, was shot and killed in Las Vegas on September 7, 1994, in what became one of hip-hop's most enduring mysteries. The rapper was among the best-selling music artists of all time, with over 75 million records sold worldwide, and was renowned not only for his musical influence but also for his outspoken activism addressing social injustice and the marginalization of African Americans. His death, along with The Notorious B.I.G.'s murder six months later, defined an era of gang-related violence in the music industry.

According to Rolling Stone, McDonald's refusal to answer questions during the Davis trial reflected a recurring challenge in the case: witnesses connected to the shooting have long remained silent, bound by street codes or fear of retaliation. Davis, who was arrested in 2023 after decades of investigation, has been accused of involvement in Tupac's death. The prosecution's case relies heavily on testimony from individuals with direct knowledge of the crime, making witness cooperation essential to establishing guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

McDonald's cryptic statement—that he would not provide answers that might "send him to prison"—suggests he believes his testimony could expose him to criminal liability. This dynamic illustrates the tension inherent in cases where potential accomplices or associates are called to testify. Without their cooperation, prosecutors struggle to reconstruct the events of that fatal night in Las Vegas.

The trial represents a rare moment of accountability in a murder that has haunted the hip-hop community and American culture for three decades. Yet the willingness of witnesses to invoke their constitutional protections underscores how difficult it remains to pierce the silence surrounding street violence, even when decades have passed and fresh investigative efforts have finally brought charges.

title: Watch ZZ Top Perform ‘Tush’ at Band’s Final Concert With Original Lineup
summary: This July 18, 2021, gig in Louisville, Kentucky, marked the end of one of the single most enduring lineups in rock history
whatHappening: ZZ Top performed 'Tush' at their final concert with the classic original lineup on July 18, 2021, in Louisville, Kentucky. The show marked the end of a five-decade run with the same three musicians who defined the band's sound.
whoInvolved: ZZ Top is an American rock band formed in Houston, Texas in 1969, consisting of vocalist-guitarist Billy Gibbons, drummer Frank Beard, and bassist-vocalist Dusty Hill. The trio became one of rock's most iconic and enduring lineups, known for their signature blues-based sound and distinctive visual style.
whyMatters: The concert represents a historic closing chapter for one of rock music's most stable and recognizable bands. The original lineup's five-decade run together is exceptionally rare in rock history, and this performance marked the definitive end of an era that shaped blues-rock for generations.
articleBody:
ZZ Top took the stage in Louisville, Kentucky on July 18, 2021, to perform what would become their final concert with the band's original and iconic three-member lineup. According to Rolling Stone, the performance of their 1975 hit 'Tush' from the album Fandango! captured a moment that closed one of the most remarkable chapters in rock history.

The band, formed in Houston, Texas in 1969, had maintained an extraordinary consistency that few acts in any genre have achieved. Vocalist-guitarist Billy Gibbons, drummer Frank Beard, and bassist-vocalist Dusty Hill played together for more than fifty years, creating a rhythm section and musical identity that became instantly recognizable to fans worldwide. This stability allowed the band to develop and refine a signature sound rooted in Gibbons' blues-inflected guitar work, anchored by the rock-solid partnership of Beard and Hill.

Beyond their musical output, ZZ Top became famous for their distinctive presentation. Gibbons and Hill cultivated matching appearances featuring sunglasses, hats, and long beards that became as much a part of the band's brand as their music. Combined with their sly and humorous lyrics and a reputation for electrifying live performances, the trio built a cultural footprint that extended far beyond typical rock audiences.

The Louisville show in July 2021 represented a natural culmination of an unprecedented run. Five decades with the same three members is virtually unheard of in rock music, where lineup changes, creative differences, and personal circumstances typically force evolution or dissolution. That ZZ Top maintained its core identity and continued touring and recording throughout this entire period speaks to the chemistry between Gibbons, Beard, and Hill, as well as their shared commitment to the music and their fanbase.

For longtime fans and observers of rock history, the performance carried particular weight as a farewell to a configuration that had defined not just ZZ Top's identity, but also served as a touchstone for rock stability itself. The final notes of 'Tush' in Louisville marked the end of an era that had seemed, against all odds, almost permanent.

title: C+C Music Factory Founder Sues Freedom Williams in $30 Million Trademark Lawsuit
summary: Robert Clivillés claims rapper Williams has been making money off the group's name without permission
whatHappening: Robert Clivillés, co-founder of C+C Music Factory, is suing rapper Freedom Williams for $30 million over trademark rights to the group's name. Clivillés claims Williams has been profiting from the C+C Music Factory brand without authorization.
whoInvolved: Robert Clivillés co-founded C+C Music Factory in 1989 alongside David Cole; the group became a major act in late 1980s and early 1990s dance and hip-hop music. Freedom Williams is the original lead rapper of the group's biggest hits and currently holds the trademark rights to the C+C Music Factory name, which he acquired in 2003.
whyMatters: The lawsuit highlights ongoing disputes over intellectual property and band identity in the music industry, particularly when original members disagree on who controls a group's legacy and commercial rights. The outcome could set precedent for how trademark ownership is determined among founding members of long-defunct musical acts.
articleBody:
Robert Clivillés, the co-founder of the 1990s dance and hip-hop group C+C Music Factory, has filed a $30 million trademark lawsuit against rapper Freedom Williams, alleging that Williams has been using and profiting from the group's name without permission. According to Rolling Stone, Clivillés claims that Williams has made substantial income from touring and other commercial activities under the C+C Music Factory banner.

C+C Music Factory was established in 1989 by Clivillés and David Cole and rose to prominence with a string of hit singles including "Gonna Make You Sweat," "Here We Go," "Things That Make You Go Hmmm...," "Just a Touch of Love," and "Keep It Comin'." Williams, who served as the group's lead rapper on these tracks, became closely associated with the act's commercial success. The band ceased recording following Cole's death in 1996, though the group later reformed in 2010 with Eric Kupper stepping in to replace Cole.

The crux of the dispute centers on trademark ownership. Williams acquired the legal rights to the C+C Music Factory name in 2003 and has continued to tour and perform under that banner. Clivillés's lawsuit contests Williams's exclusive right to use the name, arguing that the original co-founder and his estate should retain ownership or at least control over how the brand is commercialized.

The case underscores longstanding tensions within the music industry over artistic identity and intellectual property when founding members of successful groups pursue divergent paths. While Williams has the registered trademark, Clivillés's legal challenge suggests he believes the co-founder's original creative contribution entitles him to a stake in the group's commercial exploitation. The $30 million figure reflects the perceived value of the C+C Music Factory brand and its enduring appeal to audiences decades after the group's original run.

title: Stella Lefty Finds Guidance From SZA and Liberation in Stevie Knicks

articleBody:
Stella Lefty is opening up about the artists and songs that have shaped her creative vision. In an interview with Rolling Stone for the publication's Song Shuffle Series, the "Boston" singer walked through a playlist that spans decades and genres, revealing the breadth of her musical education.

According to Rolling Stone, the Song Shuffle Series invites artists to discuss their influences through a carefully chosen selection of songs, creating a window into their artistic development. This mixing of old and new reflects a growing trend among emerging artists who view musical history not as a rigid timeline but as an interconnected landscape of inspiration.

Lefty's inclusion of artists like Elvis Presley and Thomas Rhett suggests her engagement with American popular music across multiple eras and genres. Rather than confining herself to a single lane, she appears to be building a personal mythology that honors both groundbreaking women in rock and pop and the storytelling traditions of country music. The "Boston" singer's openness about these diverse influences positions her within a lineage of artists who see genre boundaries as porous and creative collaboration as essential to artistic growth.

Through conversations like this, emerging artists use the platform to educate listeners about their own references and to signal their place within broader musical conversations. title: Shakira Pledges $1.25 Million to Rebuild Schools Damaged by Earthquake in Colombia
summary: The Colombian singer's Fundación Pies Descalzos will lead an effort to kickstart education in the devastated Chocó region
whatHappening: Shakira is committing $1.25 million to rebuild schools destroyed by an earthquake in Colombia's Chocó region. Her foundation, Fundación Pies Descalzos, will lead the reconstruction and education recovery effort in the affected area.
whoInvolved: Shakira, the Colombian singer and humanitarian, is backing the initiative through Fundación Pies Descalzos (the Barefoot Foundation), a charity she founded in 1997 dedicated to providing quality education to poor and vulnerable Colombian children. The effort targets the Chocó Department, a Pacific region home to the nation's largest Afro-Colombian population.
whyMatters: The pledge addresses critical infrastructure damage to schools in an already vulnerable region, helping restore educational access to displaced and marginalized communities. This intervention is significant both for immediate recovery and for the foundation's long-term mission to ensure every Colombian child can exercise their right to quality education.
articleBody:
Shakira is pledging $1.25 million to rebuild schools devastated by an earthquake in Colombia's Chocó region, marking a major humanitarian response to the natural disaster. The Colombian singer's Fundación Pies Descalzos will lead the effort to restore educational infrastructure and restart programs in the affected area, according to Rolling Stone.

The Barefoot Foundation, established by Shakira in 1997, has long focused on helping poor and impoverished children across Colombia. The organization's stated mission centers on ensuring that every Colombian child can exercise their right to a quality education, with a particular emphasis on serving displaced and vulnerable communities by addressing their unique needs. This latest commitment reflects that core mandate.

Chocó Department, located in Colombia's Pacific region, is home to the largest Afro-Colombian population in the nation, alongside significant populations of Amerindian and mixed African-Amerindian Colombians. The region's geography is distinctive—it is the only Colombian department with coastlines on both the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean, and it contains all of Colombia's border with Panama. Its capital is Quibdó. The area has historically faced economic challenges and infrastructure gaps, making earthquake recovery particularly difficult for local communities.

The earthquake damage to schools in Chocó represents a severe setback for educational access in a region already struggling with resource constraints. By pledging $1.25 million toward reconstruction, Shakira's foundation aims to accelerate the restoration of learning spaces and enable students to return to classrooms. The commitment underscores the foundation's broader effort to support education in Colombia's most underserved areas.

The rebuilding initiative will not only address physical infrastructure but also help stabilize education systems disrupted by the disaster. For students in Chocó, restoring schools represents a pathway back to normalcy and continuity in their learning. The foundation's targeted approach to vulnerable and displaced communities positions it to understand and meet the specific needs of earthquake-affected families in the region.
